Since I needed this program for a different project, I implemented most of this utility program (basemapper.py). This program is based on one I wrote years ago for a much bigger project. I pulled out the parts I needed, basically the multi-threaded file downloader. This program support several upstream sources for map tiles, and caches them to disk where they can be used as a TMS source by JOSM or QGIS, which lets you work fully offline. That part is working well.

What's left to do is adding the code to generate the mbtiles file from the tiles. Ideally I'll also add creating an sqlitedb file for Osmand, which is very similar to mbtiles.
I think this needs some of the work flow I documented in the same doc for my odkconvert project.

The odkconvert program can generate OSM XML and GeoJson from either a CSV file downloaded from Central, or the raw XML instance file copied off your device. This will need to be incorporated into the backend and front-end. For now it's terminal based, but all the work is done in classes, so easy to use from other programs.

This is done. It doesn't cache anything in memory, so can handle large areas. In addition to making an XYZ map tile cache on disk, it can also  create mbtiles for ODK Collect, and sqlitedb files for Osmand. It's multi-threaded, so fast. It takes a polygon as the boundary, and then the imagery source.

Ivan's instructions to generate forms:

Steps:
1. Navigate to the fmtm git repo on your local
2. Activate the venv (source venv/bin/activate) (need to ensure you have openpyxl and segno installed, which should be the case if the requirements.txt has been installed by pip)
3. use tasks2forms, with two arguments:
  a. Root folder of the project
  b. The xlsform template
4. Now you should have a folder full of xforms
5. run forms2server with 4 arguments:
  a. Root folder of the project
  b. ODK server URL
  c. ODK server username
  d. ODK server password

This surprisingly works, but it wasn't really obvious. The new conflation program does work with a POI from ODK Collect, whereas in OSM all the tags are on the building polygon. The program successfully updates existing tags if the value from ground-truthing is different, and merges the two sets of tags together as part of the building polygon. This only works with JOSM, as the data file FMTM has all modified features tagged as modified in OSM, and the version number increased. Then the result only needs to be visually validated before uploading.

This turned out to be really easy. I looked into using pandas to read the spreadsheet, but it was not an optimal solution. As I have parsed many XML files before using xmltodict, that was used to change the version and task name, and the data extract file name. The advantage here is one of performance. Rather than editing the XLSForm source file, and running xls2xform for each task, this only requires conversion once.

The initial implementation of this just generates a square grid, as this is needed for the project to work at all. This can be improved in the future, possible supporting multiple splitting schemes, but this will have to come later.
This program is actually part of the odkconvert project, but the backend needs to support creating this extract so it can be uploaded with the modified XForm.

  There are several incentive mechanisms that can be used to encourage new contributors to participate in a research project. Some of the most common ones include:

Contributor Rewards: This is a common incentive mechanism that involves providing financial or other tangible rewards to contributors who contribute to the research project. Rewards can be in the form of cash, gift cards, or other types of incentives that can motivate contributors to participate.

Badges and Recognition: Providing badges and recognition to contributors who make significant contributions to the project can also be a great way to incentivize new contributors. Badges and recognition can be displayed on the contributor's profile page or social media, and can provide a sense of achievement and recognition for their work.

Gamification: Gamification is the use of game design principles to incentivize and motivate contributors. It can involve using leaderboards, achievements, and other game mechanics to encourage participation and engagement.

Community Engagement: Engaging contributors in the research community can also be an effective way to incentivize new contributors. This can involve providing opportunities for contributors to network, collaborate, and share their work with others in the research community.

Training and Development: Providing training and development opportunities to new contributors can also be a powerful incentive mechanism. This can involve providing access to training resources, mentorship, or other types of professional development opportunities that can help contributors build their skills and advance in their careers.

Overall, the key to incentivizing new contributors is to provide a variety of different mechanisms that can appeal to different types of contributors. By offering a range of rewards, recognition, and development opportunities, research projects can attract and retain a diverse and talented group of contributors.

1.2. Explore implementation of the [AllContributors Bot](https://allcontributors.org/docs/en/bot/installation) https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/issues/83 or research other alternatives
The AllContributors Bot is a useful tool for managing contributors to open-source projects. It automates the process of adding contributors to a project's README file and helps to recognize the contributions made by individuals. Here's how you can explore the implementation of the AllContributors Bot:

First, you'll need to have a GitHub account and access to a repository where you want to add the bot.

Go to the AllContributors Bot GitHub repository (https://github.com/all-contributors/all-contributors-bot) and read the README file to understand how the bot works.

Next, you can follow the instructions in the "Getting Started" section to add the bot to your repository. This involves granting the bot access to your repository and adding a configuration file.

Once you have added the bot, it will automatically generate a table of contributors in your project's README file, based on the information in your repository. You can customize the table to display different types of contributions, such as code, documentation, and translations.

You can also use the bot to manually add contributors to the table. To do this, you can use the following command in a pull request comment:
``
@all-contributors please add <username> for <contribution type>
For example, if you want to add a contributor named "Alice" for their code contributions, you can use the following comment:

``
@all-contributors please add alice for code
The bot will then automatically update the table in your README file to include the new contributor.
Alternatively, if you are looking for other alternatives, you can consider using other GitHub apps like the "contributors" app by Github, which automatically generates a contributors list for your repository. Another option is to use a static site generator like Jekyll, Hugo, or Gatsby that has built-in support for generating contributors' lists. Lastly, you can write your own script or program to generate a contributors list based on the information in your repository.

Thank you for the clarification. I’ve learnt something new! I’ll look into making it more high level with extra details.

1. First we need to create a test client for calling our FastAPI endpoints, which we could do as a pytest fixture in tests/conftest.py:

```python
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def test_client():
    """FastAPI test client for endpoint testing."""
    return TestClient(app)
```
 
2. Then for endpoints which use ODKCentral, we need to also mock the request to it internally, using `requests-mock` (https://pypi.org/project/requests-mock):

e.g.

```python
from backend.config import settings

@requests_mock.Mocker()
def test_list_odk_central_projects(client):
    project_json = {VALID_PROJECTS_JSON_HERE}
    m.get(f"{settings.ODK_CENTRAL_URL}/url/projects", json=project_json)
    response = client.get("/projects")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == project_json
```

I haven't tested the code above, but it's just an example of what you could do.
Most endpoints require some form of ODKCentral request, but for those that don't, it would be an easy first test (simply using TestClient and validating the response).

Hi @mohammadareeb95, thanks for contributing!

### Issue 1 is in two parts:

**a)** Simplify ODKCentral API Dockerfile, removing manual database variable injection.

I recently made a PR to ODKCentral that allows environment variables to be passed for the database credentials (https://github.com/getodk/central/pull/389). The variables are DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_NAME.

The whole section https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/blob/ae5cb0651b0e979e55a613e51e04d1c69ef2f82e/odkcentral/api/Dockerfile#L59 could be removed from the API Dockerfile, and environment variables passed during ODKCentral start instead.

**b)** Override entrypoint for the ODKCentral API Dockerfile.

Currently we need to run two commands on first API start, to create an ODKCentral user and promote them to admin: https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/wiki/DEV-2.-Backend#1b-setup-odk-central-user

We need to look into the ODKCentral docs to find a way to do this without requiring a prompt (e.g. with password directly on command line).

Then we could create a new entrypoint for the Dockerfile, which inits the admin user, then **exec**s the existing entrypont:
"./wait-for-it.sh", "${CENTRAL_DB_HOST:-central-db}:5432", "--", "./sub-db-vars.sh"


### Issue 2 is simpler

We just need a way to run `docker-compose up -d` with an option for not running ODKCentral and the additional proxy.

One way to solve this could be with a separate docker compose file that doesn't have the sections included (e.g. docker-compose.noodk.yml).

`.env.dev` in the subdirectories isn't required (if you need it for something else, please add to .gitignore). Variables injected by docker compose should be read from `.env` in the repo root.

Also the Dockerfile under each directory requires hardcoding the URL to the production values, due to how our building is configured with quay.io (build args cannot be passed).

Otherwise looks great to me!

pdm run uvicorn main:api --reload

FROM node:12-slim
    
    WORKDIR /app
    
    COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
    
    RUN yarn install --frozen-lockfile --non-interactive --production=true && \
        yarn cache clean
    
    COPY . .
    
    ENV NODE_ENV production
    ENV PORT 80
    ENV REDIS_URL redis://redis:6379
    ENV SESSION_SECRET your-session-secret
    ENV DB_HOST central-db
    ENV DB_USER central_admin
    ENV DB_PASSWORD admin_password
    ENV DB_NAME central
    ENV ADMIN_EMAIL admin@example.com
    ENV ADMIN_PASSWORD admin_password
    
    EXPOSE 80
    
    COPY entrypoint.sh /
    RUN chmod +x /entrypoint.sh
    
    ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]
    CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]

In this Dockerfile, a new script called entrypoint.sh is added that initializes the admin user and then runs the original entrypoint command. The entrypoint.sh script will be something like this:
      #!/bin/bash
      
      set -e
      
      # Create admin user
      node src/bin/add-admin-user.js
      
      # Run original entrypoint command
      ./wait-for-it.sh ${CENTRAL_DB_HOST:-central-db}:5432 -- ./sub-db-vars.sh
      
      exec "$@"

This script
-  first initializes the admin user using the add-admin-user.js script
- then runs the original entrypoint command that waits for the database to be ready and substitutes database variables using wait-for-it.sh and sub-db-vars.sh.


To use this updated Dockerfile, you can build the image with:
`docker build -t odkcentral-api .`

And then start a container with:
`docker run -it --rm odkcentral-api`

This will automatically initialize the admin user and start the ODKCentral API server.

Yep, we need an action for prod and an action for dev. 

They are very similar, but have different triggers.

SQLAlchemy is a great package. While there is a small performance overhead compared to using the driver directly, I think the trade off is worth it.

If we use psycopg directly, I'm not sure how we could manage the database models in a maintainable way. We currently also rely in automatic database migration (creation) on the first start of FMTM (e.g. for local dev servers), and this relies on SQLAlchemy.

I think we'll be doing this in a much simpler way, and just load an sql file that's a dump of the schema. Other than using sqlalchemy to create the database, I was using the lower level function to execute SQL anyway. This will also make it easier to create test cases, since they'll all need to create a database with test data. It's not a performance issue, mostly just reducing complexity since pretty soon we'll be doing major triage on the schema.

This idea is growing on me.

## Work required

I estimate we currently have about 10 database queries to re-write in pure SQL, to be able to remove SQLAlchemy - I could work on this after finishing the docker config I am working on.

## Additional benefits

- Obviously this would make database queries marginally quicker / reduce overhead.
- We could also shift driver to use asyncpg or psycopg3 (fully async, also faster, fits better with FastAPI).
- A side advantage is that we can make Postgis queries directly on the DB, instead of using GeoAlchemy (which I have always found to be lacklustre, plus another dependency).

## For consideration

- I would actually propose we strip out the geo functionality from the FMTM API completely, and instead use: https://github.com/CrunchyData/pg_featureserv.
  - pg_featureserv is a tiny http wrapper around Postgis, allowing us to make complex queries using the OGC Features spec.
  - It's also written in Golang and should be much faster than any Python queries we write.
  - It also helps us use a more micro-service based approach, reducing the complexity of the FMTM API itself.

I made a start this evening using psycopg3.

I slightly underestimated the task - it's a pretty big refactor, but I do think the end result is easy to understand. 

The downside is that we lose the overview of what tables and fields are present in the DB. Plus the ORM provides centralisation of tables and fields that we don't get with raw SQL (updating or adding a new field requires updating in multiple places).

We would also have to be wary of SQL injection on raw queries. This risk is reduced by passing in params instead of substituting variables directly into the string.

Note 1: We can use pooling of connections with psycopg and probably even use async queries. 

Note 2: I stripped out a lot of unused dependencies and updated others (I had never actually gone through the package list we inherited before).

sqlalchemy is overkill. It is designed to support multiple different databases, but we'll only use postgres due it it having postgis. I agree that if we continue using sqlalchemy alembic makes sense, but I prefer not adding more layers of dependencies. Sam was about to do this refactoring from sqlalchemy, so this is a good time to talk about the path forward.

SQLAlchemy is good, and has some advantages, but we don't necessarily need the abstraction. Raw SQL gives more flexibility, easier use of complex queries, and potential performance optimisation.

Look into some comparisons online. Each has their use case, but I think we will rely a lot on raw SQL when using Postgis anyway & we don't need to portability provided by an ORM (we will likely always use Postgres). 
**Edit** example comparison https://lyz-code.github.io/blue-book/architecture/orm_builder_query_or_raw_sql/

I think a good middle ground here could be to use a query builder. The SQL can be generated using familiar Python syntax and then executed directly by the postgres driver. This also protects against SQL injection. 

Something I have not tested, but could suit us nicely is: https://github.com/samuelcolvin/buildpg. It's by the creator for Pydantic and has a nice integration with asyncpg too.

On a side note: asyncpg vs psycopg3. Either will do the job, but asyncpg will likely always be more performant. Here is a good blog post by the creator of psycopg suggesting they will prioritise compatibility with psycopg2 and ease of use over performance: https://www.varrazzo.com/blog/2020/05/19/a-trip-into-optimisation/

And then finally we have database migrations to deal with. A pretty simple approach is to make a `migrations` directory containing sequential text or .sql files with the SQL logic required for each migration. It's the way I have handled it in some other projects I work on.

I have nothing against migration tools like alembic, as I have never had issues. Others complain that they can't handle complex migrations and have a lack of transparency. Text file migrations are pretty simple and easy to understand, plus have one less dependency to worry about.

Right now we're already using a query generator. All queries have a YAML config file in the data_models directory. Then the backend converts it to the different queries for local postgres, remote Underpass, and Overpass. My main reason for refactoring to psycopg3 is long term maintenance. I also have usually just have an SQL file of the schema, and a simple script to handle migrations. We'll only be using postgres, so the additional overhead and flexibility of sqlalchemy isn't needed.

This adds a lot more context, as fmtm relies heavily on osm-fieldwork. I think it makes complete sense to move away from SQLAlchemy as we generate raw SQL for the most important logic anyway.

For basic CRUD in fmtm we could use raw SQL too.
My main concerns were:

- SQL injection (as this is a web API, not a lower level package). If contributors don't write SQL property with variable substitution, then we could have an attacker drop all data (we need backups), access hidden data (not a major concern).

- Development friendliness. SQLAlchemy is pretty ubiquitous in the Python development world and reasonably easy to pick up. In an ideal world everyone would know SQL, but sometimes this isn't the case.

After discussion with Rob, we decided that using a combination of raw SQL (for very complex queries), and a query generator (for simple queries), would be a good approach.

We also discussed asyncpg vs psycopg3, and it makes sense to go with whatever is the most performant and well adopted.
In this case it's actually asyncpg.

I suggest we give https://github.com/samuelcolvin/buildpg a try (which combines query generation with asyncpg).

The model for organization is:
```python
class Organisation(BaseModel):
    slug: str
    logo: str
    name: str
    description: str
    url: str
    type: int
```

**Solution**:
- We need to generate the slug param from the name, probably just a computed property with `name.toLowerCase()` will do for now.
- The slug should be included in the POSTed formData: https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/blob/d11de09d4306e3dd2bc3a25b10d56870bc99d544/src/frontend/main/src/views/CreateOrganization.tsx#LL21C5-L21C13

### Image upload

- The issue around images that Rob posted is also a problem.
- We appear to be saving the uploaded logo image to /app/images/ on the API server.
- This isn't good practice, as restarting the server would result in losing the uploaded image.

tl;dr the image should be saved somewhere outside of the API server container to be persistent (and avoid file permission errors).

**Solution options**:
1. One option is to add the image to the database blob storage, then write an endpoint for getting images from the database. The URL provided in the organization model would be the endpoint url for getting the image.
2. Upload the image to an external object storage such as S3. This is the preferred option, but I'm not sure we have the infrastructure in place / this requires talks with IT to provision the S3.
3. Probably the most realistic: create a docker volume under /app/images that will persist on container restart (I can help with this).

I think Celery may be overkill. There are two kinds of threading in applications. One is you fire up a background thread, and just let it run til completion, for example how submissions get downloaded now. There is no communication needed with the spawning application.

The other type is where all the threads have to communicate, so you need a message passing layer. That's what Celery would supply, but I don't think we need it. For basemap production, it's already multi-threaded internally. For other background tasks, if there is no need to communication, then I wouldn't bother with Celery.

Performance will be terrible for large projects using GeoJSON.

I would suggest we try using PMTiles - they are perfect for this use case.
They are basically just MBTiles, but with better optimisation for the web.
(MBTiles are SQLite based, made to work offline. PMTiles use HTTP RANGE requests to only access the data they need on demand).

During project creation we could generate a PMTiles output of all boundaries, and host it on S3.
More info on generating PMTiles here: https://github.com/hotosm/raw-data-api/issues/136
The S3 URL is stored in the database for direct access by the frontend (this will be fast).

## Prerequisite
- This will probably be after the tech team meetup, as it needs S3 hosted on AWS or Azure.

## Additional Considerations
- We need to factor in styling too. It should be similar for MBTiles and PMTiles output.

Anyway, it can be done. But instead of instantiating the log during every call of the endpoint, the log should be instantiated once at FastAPI startup then hooked / filtered in the endpoint.

So add the extra log in main.py to a file you choose, with enqueue=True to make this non-blocking for async and a filter on a specific task type =project_create

Then in the endpoint bind task=project_create to any logs that you wish to also add to this extra file.

## Note

Also be aware you will lose this log file on container restart.

**Some thoughts for a potential solution to solve both the offline basemap and large geojson issues**:

1. Project is created with task boundaries.
2. File outputs are generated on S3 inside directory structure like `/bucket/<project_id>/FILES`:
  - PMTiles: `basemap.pmtiles`: underlying tile layer (osm, satellite, drone).
  - Flatgeobuf: `boundaries.flatgeobuf`: project boundary, task boundaries, and OSM data extract within each task boundary.
3. When user has connectivity, they can just use the (bandwidth efficient, cached) PMTiles without issue.
4. When a user clicks to download files for offline usage on a specific task:
  - The tiles in the task AOI are extracted from the `.pmtiles` using Python [aiopmtiles](https://github.com/developmentseed/aiopmtiles) (this could be a Lambda function, or a FastAPI function).
  - Tiles are packaged up as `.mbtiles` for use in either FMTM mobile app offline, or in ODKCollect (via [filepicker idea in the ODK forum](https://forum.getodk.org/t/provide-a-way-to-get-mbtiles-to-collect-without-having-to-connect-to-a-computer/42206/9))

5. The user goes mapping in their task area with FMTM for navigation, selecting a building.

Related to user permissions / roles implementation: #902

## FMTM Roles

We discussed this morning.
I think the roles Rob proposed are ideal - we just added one more role:

- **Super Admin** - not a db role, the person that has ssh keys and direct database access.
- **Admin** - permission for everything on FMTM, but no database access.
- **Organisation Admin** - all permissions within an organisation, to create projects, grant project admin roles, but not mess with other organisation projects.
- **Project Admin** - can modify / delete project, grant permissions to field admins, mappers, etc.
- **Field Admin** (associate project admin, with a nicer name) - cannot delete or modify the project, but can grant users access to projects, and unlock tasks.
- **Mapper** - can map tasks and that's it (default).
- **Validator** - can modify tasks worked on by mappers, download all submissions, push data to OSM.

Now the question is, how does this fit in with Tasking Managers idea of Team based permissions?

The end goal is to have a user management module that handles all of this - it needs to work for both FMTM and TM (either using the same schema, or having a mapping between the two).

## TM Roles

- The first level of roles is an enum: mapper, admin, blocked user (read only).
- Mappers are granted admin rights by another admin.
- Levels of admin:
  - Organisation
  - Team
  - Campaign

We may have another meeting with @ramyaragupathy to clarify and discuss how to best map FMTM --> TM roles.

So to address your questions:

### 1) Download the data extract generated by FMTM

- Once https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/issues/934 is implemented then this should be trivial.
- The data extract will be available in flatgeobuf format on the raw-data-api S3 bucket (with a URL that won't change.
- We can add a link to the S3 URL in our database, for reference.
- However, as the URL is in a consistent format using the project id, we don't need to get the URL from the backend to download.
- A user clicks download and the frontend just redirects to the URL in the standard format `S3_URL/fmtm/{project_id}/hotosm-fmtm-project-{project_id}.fgb`.
- Note: we could possibly also specify to download only a  **subset** of the data (i.e. with a bbox specified).

### 2) Update and modify the data and re-upload

- If the data extract isn't exactly how we would like, we can go back and tweak the params and regenerate  the extract (it will be replaced on the raw-data-api S3 bucket, under the same URL).
- If it's still not good enough using the filters on raw-data-api, then we can give the user the option to upload a custom data extract (we need this functionality anyway for some users).
  - We should have a small endpoint that accepts this new extract, then uploads it to **our** S3 bucket, also inserting the URL into the database.
  - The uploaded data extract would have to be parsed and ideally converted to flatgeobuf for efficient access.

## Summary / TODO

Once https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/issues/934 is complete, we need to:

- Update the **frontend** to have a button for downloading the extract from a URL like: `S3_URL/fmtm/{project_id}/hotosm-fmtm-project-{project_id}.fgb`.
- Update the **backend** to accept a custom data extract, parse, convert to flatgeobuf, then upload to our S3 bucket, and replace the link in the DB.

There are two issues to consider here:

### 1 Event Loop Blocking

- Running as async function within the background task will run it in the asyncio event loop.
- If there are no more workers to handle the request (set to 4), then FastAPI will hang.

More context here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/67599119/fastapi-asynchronous-background-tasks-blocks-other-requests

### 2 Cancelling Jobs

- We track background jobs in our DB (background_tasks table).
- Their status is updated when complete.
- BackgroundTasks cannot be easily stopped though. 
- Ideally we need a way to collect running background tasks associated with an endpoint (tagged with project ID), then cancel existing jobs if the user cancels, goes back, refreshes, etc.

### Possible Solution

We discussed using celery before & agreed it's too heavyweight. 

I agree - scalability is also a pain, so using the database to manage tasks is a better solution IMO.

[apscheduler](https://github.com/agronholm/apscheduler) looks like a good tool for our use case, to replace the simple BackgroundTasks.

It allows for tasks to be cancelled, paused, resumed. It could probably be implemented ourselves, but this is simple.

It can be set up with FastAPI asyncio loop:

```python
from apscheduler.schedulers.asyncio import AsyncIOScheduler

sched = AsyncIOScheduler()
sched.start()
```

Then jobs can be spawned from called endpoints with an ID associated (note no async).

```python
def job():
    sched.add_job(download_tiles, "date", run_date=datetime.now(), args=[], id=<unique_id>
    # to stop: sched.remove_job(<unique_id>)
```

The job ids are stored in the BackgroundTasks table as the primary key, for reference if the user triggers the process again on the frontend (i.e. with tweaked params).

> Note we need an endpoint to cancel tasks, taking the project ID as a param. Then when the user navigates back, or triggers the task again, we can call this endpoint to delete the tasks.

6) We have two options:

### Option 1: Validate Data Extract during Project Creation

- When 'Use OSM data extract' is selected, the user clicks a button like 'Get data'.
- This takes some time to process / download via osm-rawdata.
- The extract will be generated as flatgeobuf, so could be viewed immediately in the map on the right (for inspection by the user).
- The advantage is immediate validation by the user, but the disadvantage is waiting time (slows down the project creation flow).
- My concern here is that if we generate the data extract, then the user abandons the project creation, we will have a generated extract that will persist in S3, but isn't linked to a project.

### Option 2: Validate Data Extract after Project Creation

- This has worse UX, but may be more practical (testing will let us know).
- The user continues with project creation to the end.
- The data extract is generated and validated.
- If the data extract is not valid, the user is informed (the project flagged), and they have to go back and update the project creation values to try again.

There are 3 different triggers in apscheduler.
1. Interval trigger: Schedules a job to run at fixed intervals.
2. Cron trigger
    Schedules a job based on a cron-like expression.
    Options: year, month, day, week, day_of_week, hour, minute, second: Specify the cron expression.
3. Date trigger.
    Schedules a job to run once at a specific date and time.

Date trigger is the best one for our use case, but it creates the job in the db and then removes it immediately after the job is started.

Are there any other triggers that I have missed?

## Using apscheduler

@nrjadkry has done some great research into this.

Apscheduler is actually quite limited:
- It creates a db table with: id, next_run_time, and task_state.
- Scheduled jobs can be cancelled before they run.
- Jobs that are currently running cannot be cancelled (it just cancelled via the db, nothing special with asyncio task cancellation).

**So apscheduler is probably not suitable for our needs.**

## Original Requirements

### Not blocking the event loop when we run create_project

This can be solved by using a def for now instead of async def and it will run in another thread.

### Terminate a running create_project instance (this issue)

This is lower priority for now in my opinion.
We will keep this issue open to address it in the future.

In summary:

- This is partly about trust. We should hope that a user won't intentionally spam the project_create endpoint and hang the server (when we test by calling it repeatedly, it's not a realistic scenario).
- When the user submits the form to create a project, the form should be cleared so they cannot accidentally submit the same job twice.
- This can potentially be handled in the future by using `asyncio.create_task` instead.
  - A name can be assigned to the asyncio job.
  - Then the task can be cancelled either by an endpoint call, or when project_create is triggered twice in a row (previous is still running).
  - Ref: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64764679/how-to-cancel-asyncio-tasks-by-name

## Optimal Solution

So I think the **optimal** approach would be using flatgeobuf data within a sozip file (for compression).
This does add complexity, however.

I have written a function `app.db.postgis_utils.geojson_to_flatgeobuf` that takes a geojson FeatureCollection and converts it to a flatgeobuf object, directly in the postgis database!

I wanted to avoid having to add GDAL to the FMTM API for now (it's in the database).

However, stupidly, I neglected to think about reading the data: we can read and write entire flatgeobuf files using postgis, but when it comes to reading we want to have access to GDAL to use HTTP RANGE requests on the flatgeobuf object (accessing only what we need).

### A Compromise

I think for now we should use a compromise.

Having the submissions and metadata neatly in a flatgeobuf file would be awesome, but let's keep it simple for now and just use the JSON as implemented in this PR (downloading the entire file every time).

The metadata (submission count, etc) should just be accessed from the db as we do currently.

## Note for the future

As a thought: we don't necessarily need flatgeobuf reading from the backend.

In the future we could write the data with the function I wrote, then do the reading entirely in the browser, where there is good support with the [flatgeobuf package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/flatgeobuf)

Note: the function can be used like this:

```python
import geojson
from app.db.postgis_utils import geojson_to_flatgeobuf
from io import BytesIO

@router.post("/something")
async def something(
    upload_geojson: UploadFile = File(...),
    db: Session = Depends(database.get_db),
):
    json_obj = await upload_geojson.read()
    parsed_geojson = geojson.loads(json_obj)
    flatgeobuf = BytesIO(geojson_to_flatgeobuf(db, parsed_geojson))
    *do something with flatgeobuf file*
```

I have divided roles into two types:

**UserRole**:
- One of three types and is used for site-wide permissions.
  - ADMIN (super admin)
  - MAPPER (most users)
  - READ_ONLY (write access blocked)
- This is used for `user.role` in the database.

**ProjectRole**:
- Related to project specific permissions.
- Stored in `user_roles` link table, with the `project_id` and `user_id` being a composite primary key.
  - This means the user can multiple roles across projects (multiple entries in the table).
  - BUT, can only have _one role within a project_.
- This is where we define the roles like org admin, project admin, validator, etc.

The role types are used differently.
The role `user.role` is only used to designate super admin & block users.
The roles under `user_roles` are specific to projects.

There is confusion between UserRole and ProjectRole here - I really don't like how we had to reuse the Tasking Manager schema, but we are stuck with it.

**UserRole** is one of three options: ADMIN, MAPPER, READ_ONLY. This applies site-wide and is mostly used to either block users, or allow admin access (the label of 'MAPPER' is just the default everyone gets - it would be better named 'USER').

**ProjectRole** is roles specific to a project:
```
        - MAPPER = default for all
        - VALIDATOR = can validate the mappers output
        - FIELD_MANAGER = can invite mappers and organise people
        - ASSOCIATE_PROJECT_MANAGER = helps the project manager, cannot delete project
        - PROJECT_MANAGER = has all permissions to manage a project
```

So for the question you asked, first we check the `users.role` entry to see if they are admin, or blocked (READ_ONLY).
If neither is true, then we check the org permission (`organisation_managers` table).
If they are not an org admin, then we check the project specific permission (`user_roles` table).

This looks like good work, but I'm not sure we need a new table for comments.
I think the idea of the `task_history` table is that is it's used for various events, including comments (this is what tasking manager does anyway).
See https://github.com/hotosm/fmtm/issues/241#issuecomment-1919535357

Options for the `taskaction` enum, which is used in `task_history`:
```
CREATE TYPE public.taskaction AS ENUM (
    'RELEASED_FOR_MAPPING',
    'LOCKED_FOR_MAPPING',
    'MARKED_MAPPED',
    'LOCKED_FOR_VALIDATION',
    'VALIDATED',
    'MARKED_INVALID',
    'MARKED_BAD',
    'SPLIT_NEEDED',
    'RECREATED',
    'COMMENT'
);
```

I am open to the idea, but don't want to deviate from the TM schema very much (especially considering Robs work on tm-admin).

There are pydantic models in task_schemas for TaskHistory that could be used for input (they may need to be tweaked).
But for the comment output/display, we could use the models you made with a little workaround:

```python
class TaskCommentRequest(BaseModel):
    """Task mapping history."""

    action_text: Any = Field(exclude=True)

    task_id: int
    project_id: int
    comment: Optional[str] = None

    @field_serializer("comment")
    def convert_action_to_comment(self, value: str) -> Optional[str]:
        """Get the task history comment."""
        if self.action_text:
            return self.action_text
        return None
```

This way when you create the pydantic model from the database (sqlalchemy) model, the `action_text` will be included in the model, but the actual serialised JSON will not include `action_text` (but `comment` instead`).

Not saying we **have** to do it this way, just giving an option 😉

# OS Level Hack with _psutil_ and _multiprocessing_

Here I have presented an hacky method where I have tracked the PID of the background tasks using **multiprocessing** and **psutil** library. Here I haven't used BackgroundTask from FastAPI though.

Wondering how much this hack is acceptable. 🤔


```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
import time, psutil, signal, os
from multiprocessing import Process

app = FastAPI()

def kill_proc_tree(pid, sig=signal.SIGTERM, include_parent=True, timeout=None, on_terminate=None):
    """Kill a process tree (including grandchildren) with signal
    "sig" and return a (gone, still_alive) tuple.
    "on_terminate", if specified, is a callback function which is
    called as soon as a child terminates.
    """
    assert pid != os.getpid(), "won't kill myself"
    parent = psutil.Process(pid)
    children = parent.children(recursive=True)
    if include_parent:
        children.append(parent)
    for p in children:
        try:
            p.send_signal(sig)
        except psutil.NoSuchProcess:
            pass
    gone, alive = psutil.wait_procs(children, timeout=timeout, callback=on_terminate)
    return (gone, alive)


def long_task(dur: int, message=""):
    time.sleep(dur)
    print(message, "==COMPLETE==")

@app.get("/bg-task/")
async def start_bg_task():
    p = Process(target=long_task, args=(1000, "PROCESS"))
    p.start()
    pid = p.pid
    return {"message": "Task Queued", "task_id":pid}

@app.get("/kill/{pid}/")
async def kill(pid:int):
    kill_proc_tree(pid)
    return {"message": "Task Exit", "task_id":pid}
```

Nice idea!

Async python works a but differently though.
Functions are coroutines (wrapped functions) that are passed to the event loop.

In this case the coroutine is not the OS level process that can be killed, but the event loop is.

So first of all we don't have a PID to identify the task & second we can't easy kill the coroutine without stopping the entire process (which is running the FastAPI server in our case).

There may still be a solution though, as I am by no means an expert in python async 😄

I **haven't use FastAPI BackgroundTask** here. Rather I have used `from multiprocessing import Process`. With this I am able to grab the PID and kill it. I have only verified it with `ps aux` command though. ```python p = Process(target=long_task, args=(1000, "PROCESS")) p.start() pid = p.pid ``` Also I changed the long_task to async and it is killed when ran with `Process` ```python async def long_task(dur: int, message=""): await asyncio.sleep(dur) print(message, "==COMPLETE==") ``` I have obtained following result:

The thing is that you are running these processes **inside** a multiprocessing process, which defeats the point of async / threading. 

Processes created with multiprocessing have their own memory space and can utilise multiple CPU cores. They also have PIDs and are killable.

Processes spawned via threading / async are not like the above. They can only run on a single core due to the GIL and each task does not have a separate PID that can be killed.

If you can make a workaround somehow not using multiprocessing (which I'm not sure is possible but feel free to test), then that's the only way.

Also I should have noted that we don't want to use multiprocessing with FastAPI and async as it's very resource inefficient. It's fully synchronous then and would easily overload the server if we start spawning processes using multiprocessing.

ThreadpoolExecutor doesn't use cores, so this won't work as expected.

Just a quick update on the meaning of hotfix @nrjadkry @Sujanadh 

A hotfix is to address a high priority bug in production that can't wait until the next deployment cycle. 

It's a method to bypass the usual processes of waiting to merge dev --> stage --> main.

So a hotfix should probably be based off the `main` branch and the PR made to the `main` branch, if it's a genuine hotfix. In this case I think it is as production could really do with this change (without adding all of the other code on dev that may introduce other bugs).

Another approach could be to make the PR to dev, then cherry pick the commit through to production. But if the code is quite out of sync between dev and main, then this can be more difficult.

After discussion we realised it may be possible to duplicate the same xform id if multiple instances of FMTM uses the same ODK Central instance.

- The solution should be to use a UUID for the xform so it's always unique.

One approach in future you can use is 'anticipating a merge', where you can checkout another branch on top of these commits.
This way you can divide the work into separate PRs without having to wait for the first to be merged.

```bash
# current branch feat-playwright-test
git checkout -b new-feat-with-playwright
# current branch new-feat-with-playwright
```

If the review of `feat-playwright-test` means that updates must be made, you can either:
- Add the updated commits to `new-feat-with-playwright` to just work on top of things.
- Commit to `feat-playwright-test`, then rebase `new-feat-with-playwright` against it to include the new commits.

This approach can work for other devs too, who can take your branch `feat-playwright-test` and build their own branch on top of it (anticipating it's merge).

@Sujanadh if the user creates a project with a multipolygon geojson, we need two things:
- The project.outline should be determined by converting multipolygon --> single polygon area that encompasses all geoms (possibly a convex hull).
- The multipolygon should work for fmtm-splitter in two possible ways:
  - We update the code in fmtm-splitter to support multipolygon. All it's doing is parsing geometries into FeatureCollection for consistency / error handling. We need to parse MultiPolygon --> FeatureCollection of Polygons.
  - Handle this conversion on the frontend, before it's passed to fmtm-splitter, converting MultiPolygon --> FeatureCollection of Polygons.

Scratch the above. We can actually handle the polygon before it gets to fmtm-splitter.

If the user uploads a multipolygon, then can do three types of splitting:
- split_by_square: merge to single polygon for fmtm-splitter.
- 'choose area as tasks': doesn't call an endpoint, passes geoms directly to create_project endpoint. So we should merge the geoms to a single polygon for the project outline.
- split_by_sql: merge into single polygon for fmtm-splitter.
  - Allows user to upload a nested Polygon inside MultiPolygon wrapper (edge case).
  - Also allows user to upload data extract as their AOI, and we wrap around that into a single polygon.
  - In the future we may possibly block the user using splitting algorithm, if multipolygon upload, via frontend.

It isn't so clear what the best approach could be.

While "the custom format is much more flexible, and while you can convert a custom format dump into an SQL format dump you can't do the reverse easily".

Custom format has the following advantages:
- Restore can be done via pg_restore, with multiple configuration flags for maximum flexibility.
- E.g. selectively restore only some tables/schema, can choose whether to include only schema, only data, or both at restore time.
- It's faster, as it can do simultaneous jobs during the restore, significantly improving restore time.

The raw SQL format has two advantages:
- For custom format you can only restore the dump file with a version of PostgreSQL that's higher (more recent). Raw SQL has such no restriction.
- Raw SQL backups can be inspected as they are plain text.

### Data Corruption

- It would appear that using the custom format has the best advantages, with the only main concern being around data corruption.
- **So as long as the custom format does not become corrupted, it would be the best option**.
- A solution to avoid (the unlikely event of) corruption, is to store the backups on S3.
- AWS has a ridiculous level of redundancy and protection against things like bit-rot.
- MinIO uses erasure coding on an object level to protect data from loss and corruption.

Closing, using the pg_dump custom format for backups seems like a good tradeoff.

The reason this has not been addressed yet is the concern that this increases the deployment complexity.

The current setup requires no external services, other than a cloud server.

Are the benefits of an AWS-based S3 frontend much more over an Nginx hosted frontend, to make this a worthwhile tradeoff?
